why: `roots:` is the cousins join key and the join is EXACT STRING EQUALITY on
the slug (see src/cousins.ts). The corpus spells the same etymon three
ways -- bare `lemma`, `lemma-<tag>`, and `<tag>-lemma` -- so two lessons
that share an etymon can fail to join, and a missing cousin panel looks
exactly like a word with no cousins yet. HL-C419.
A split cannot be detected without knowing which hyphen-separated token is
a LANGUAGE TAG and which is part of the lemma or a gloss. The corpus has
both: `-latin` (651 slugs) and `-dravidian` (63) are tags, while `-see`,
`-heart`, `-speak` and bare single letters are glosses. Nothing in a slug
distinguishes them, which is why this list exists and is checked in.
HOW THIS LIST WAS BUILT, so it can be rebuilt: every leading and trailing
hyphen-separated token across all 2403 live slugs was counted, and the
language names among them were kept. The judgement is only ever `is this
token the name of a language or language stage` -- it is never about
frequency, so a tag used once is as valid as `latin`.
ADDING A TAG IS EXPECTED. A new track brings new tags. Add it here and the
guard starts seeing that tag's splits; leave it out and slugs using it are
treated as opaque, which loses coverage but never invents a false split.
matching: A tag is matched at EITHER end of a slug, longest first, so
`old-french` wins over `french` on `corlieu-old-french`. The remainder is
the lemma. A slug with no declared tag at either end is `bare` and its
aliasesWhy: `pie` and `proto-indo-european` are the SAME language written two ways, so
they are folded together before grouping and a `dwoh-pie` /
`proto-indo-european-dwoh` pair is reported as the split it is.
Ancestor/descendant pairs are deliberately NOT aliased. `dravidian` and
`proto-dravidian` co-occur on eight lemmas, `frankish` and `germanic` on
three, `latin` and `pie` on five -- in every one of those the two tags name
genuinely different languages and a lesson may legitimately cite either.
